blocks.text: 11.3.2 Benders Decomposition

GridCap's crews cannot do every project the capital plan of lesson 6.4.2 funds. Each program has its own crews, paid for already; beyond them, the work is done on overtime (up to a quarter of the program's crews, at $15k a crew-month) or by contractors from one pool of 3 crew-months a year, at $60k, $40k or $25k a crew-month for transmission, distribution and vegetation work. Which projects to start is a yes/no question. Who does each year's work, once the projects are chosen, is a small continuous one: a linear program per year. **Benders decomposition** keeps the two apart. A **master** problem chooses the projects and carries one variable per year standing in for that year's crew cost; for each plan the master proposes, the yearly LPs report the true cost, and their dual values become rows, **Benders cuts**, that teach the master what crew work costs, for every plan at once. This lesson builds the loop, checks every cut by hand on the first plan, and checks the loop's answer against the whole model solved in one MILP.
The crew-cost layer (overtime share, prices, contractor pool) is invented for this lesson, like the budget pots of lesson 6.4.4; GridCap is a fictional utility's portfolio.
The Model
The whole model, the one Benders will split. It is lesson 11.3.1's plan model plus the crew layer.

**Sets.** $`P`$ the projects; $`Y`$ the plan's years; $`T_i`$ the start years of project $`i`$; $`M`$ the must-do projects; $`\mathcal{G}`$ the alternative groups; $`C`$ the child projects, with parent $`p(c)`$ and lag $`L_c`$; $`G`$ the programs (transmission, distribution, vegetation), and $`P_g`$ the projects of program $`g`$.

**Parameters.** $`\text{npv}_{i,t}`$, $`c_{i,k}`$ and $`B_y`$ as in lesson 11.3.1 ($k); $`m_i`$, the crew-months project $`i`$ needs in each year it is worked on; $`d_i`$, its years of work; $`K_{g,y}`$, program $`g`$'s own crew-months in year $`y`$; $`\rho = 0.25`$, the overtime share; $`q^o = 15`$, the price of an overtime crew-month ($k); $`q^c_g`$, the price of a contractor crew-month for program $`g`$ (60, 40, 25 $k); $`U = 3`$, the contractor crew-months available per year.

**Variables.** $`x_{i,t} \in \{0,1\}`$ for $`i \in P`$, $`t \in T_i`$: project $`i`$ starts in year $`t`$. For every $`g \in G`$, $`y \in Y`$, continuous: $`w_{g,y} \ge 0`$ own crew-months used, $`o_{g,y} \ge 0`$ overtime crew-months, $`h_{g,y} \ge 0`$ contractor crew-months (in code `own`, `over`, `hire`).
The crew-months program $`g`$ needs in year $`y`$ are an expression in $`x`$:
\text{need}_{g,y}(x) \;=\; \sum_{i \in P_g} \;\sum_{t \in T_i,\ t \le y < t + d_i} m_i\, x_{i,t}
**Objective.**
\max \; \sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i} \text{npv}_{i,t}\, x_{i,t} \;-\; \sum_{y \in Y} \sum_{g \in G} \bigl(q^o\, o_{g,y} + q^c_g\, h_{g,y}\bigr)
**Constraints.** The once, must, alt, after and budget rows of lesson 11.3.1, and:

`benders.monolithic` builds exactly this and solves it with HiGHS; it is the answer the loop must reach. In it the own-crew and overtime limits are written as variable bounds; in the yearly LPs below they are rows, so that each has a dual value.
Fixing the Integer Plan Leaves One Small LP per Year

Fix a plan $`\hat x`$. Every $`\text{need}_{g,y}(\hat x)`$ becomes a number, and what is left falls apart by year: nothing links 2027's crew variables to 2028's. Each year is a three-program LP, `crew_costs.year_lp`:

for g in PROGRAMS:
    own = m.add_variable(lb=0, name=f"own_{g}")
    over = m.add_variable(lb=0, name=f"over_{g}")
    hire = m.add_variable(lb=0, name=f"hire_{g}")
    cover = own + over + hire

cost += OVERTIME_PRICE * over + CONTRACT_PRICE[g] * hire
rows[f"cover_{g}"] = m.add_linear_constraint(cover >= need[g], name=f"cover_{g}")
rows[f"own_{g}"] = m.add_linear_constraint(own <= portfolio.crews[g, year], name=f"own_{g}")
rows[f"over_{g}"] = m.add_linear_constraint(
    over <= OVERTIME_SHARE * portfolio.crews[g, year], name=f"over_{g}")

rows["pool"] = m.add_linear_constraint(sum(rows.pop("hires")) <= POOL, name="pool")
m.minimize(cost)
Call its optimal value $`Q_y(\hat x)`$, the **subproblem** value: the cheapest way to staff year $`y`$'s work under plan $`\hat x`$. The whole model is then
\max_{x} \; \sum_{i,t} \text{npv}_{i,t}\, x_{i,t} \;-\; \sum_{y \in Y} Q_y(x) \qquad \text{subject to the plan rows,}

with $`Q_y(x) = +\infty`$ when no staffing covers the work. This is the move Benders makes: the continuous variables disappear into functions of the integer ones. The functions are not known as formulas, but each one can be evaluated at any plan by one LP. The five yearly LPs are independent, so they could run in parallel; on a larger model with one LP per region and year, that matters.
The Year's Duals Price Its Right-Hand Sides, and the Same Prices Bound Every Other Plan

Solve the year's LP for $`\hat x`$, and read the dual value $`\pi_r`$ of every row $`r`$ (lesson 2.3.3: the change in the optimal cost per unit increase of the row's bound). By LP duality (lesson 2.3.2) the optimal cost equals the sum of dual times bound over the rows, since every variable's only bound is zero:
Q_y(\hat x) \;=\; \sum_{g} \Bigl(\pi_{\text{cover}_g}\, \text{need}_{g,y}(\hat x) + \pi_{\text{own}_g}\, K_{g,y} + \pi_{\text{over}_g}\, \rho K_{g,y}\Bigr) + \pi_{\text{pool}}\, U

Now change the plan. The rows' bounds change (only the cover rows', through $`\text{need}`$), but the old prices stay **dual feasible**: dual feasibility does not depend on the bounds. Any dual feasible prices give a lower bound on a minimization (weak duality), so for every plan $`x`$:
Q_y(x) \;\ge\; \sum_{g} \Bigl(\pi_{\text{cover}_g}\, \text{need}_{g,y}(x) + \pi_{\text{own}_g}\, K_{g,y} + \pi_{\text{over}_g}\, \rho K_{g,y}\Bigr) + \pi_{\text{pool}}\, U

with equality at $`\hat x`$. The right side is linear in $`x`$. Give the master a variable $`\theta_y \ge 0`$ for year $`y`$'s crew cost, and this is a row the master can hold: the **optimality cut** $`\theta_y \ge \text{(right side)}`$. `benders.cut_expression` builds it with each cover row's bound written as the master's expression $`\text{need}_{g,y}(x)`$:

expr = mathopt.LinearExpression()
for g in PROGRAMS:
    expr += result.dual_values(rows[f"cover_{g}"]) * need[g]
    expr += result.dual_values(rows[f"own_{g}"]) * crews[g]
    expr += result.dual_values(rows[f"over_{g}"]) * OVERTIME_SHARE * crews[g]
return expr + result.dual_values(rows["pool"]) * POOL

`first_cuts.py` takes the master's first plan (the plan of lesson 6.4.2: no crew costs known yet, NPV 24,260) and prints, for each year, the need against the program's own crews, the LP's cost, the check that dual times bound adds up to it, and the cut:

2027  need trans 20/26  distr  5/ 9  veget  3/ 2
      crew cost  20.00   sum of dual x bound  20.00
      nonzero duals: cover_vegetation 25, own_vegetation -25, over_vegetation -10
      optimality cut: theta_2027 >= 25 need_veget(x) -55
2028  need trans 18/19  distr 12/15  veget  1/ 3
      crew cost   0.00   sum of dual x bound   0.00
      nonzero duals: none
2029  need trans 17/20  distr 14/11  veget  1/ 4
      crew cost  51.25   sum of dual x bound  51.25
      nonzero duals: cover_distribution 40, own_distribution -40, over_distribution -25
      optimality cut: theta_2029 >= 40 need_distr(x) -508.75

Check 2027 by hand. Vegetation needs 3 crew-months and has 2 of its own. Overtime may add a quarter of 2, that is 0.5, at $15k: $7.5k. The last 0.5 comes from contractors at $25k: $12.5k. Total $20k, as printed. The prices say the same thing in marginal terms: one more crew-month of vegetation work would be bought from a contractor ($`\pi_{\text{cover}} = 25`$); one more own crew-month would save a contractor's $25k ($`\pi_{\text{own}} = -25`$); one more overtime month would save the $25k contractor month but cost $15k, a net $10k ($`\pi_{\text{over}} = -10`$). The cut evaluates to $`25 \cdot 3 - 25 \cdot 2 - 10 \cdot 0.5 = 20`$ at this plan, and for any plan it is $`\theta_{2027} \ge 25\,\text{need}_{\text{veg},2027}(x) - 55`$: the master now knows that 2027's crew cost is at least $25k for every vegetation crew-month of need beyond 2.2. At need 2 the cut asks only $`\theta \ge -5`$; the bound $`\theta \ge 0`$ does the rest. A cut is exact where it was made and a bound everywhere else.
<!-- practice 1 -->
An Infeasible Year Returns a Feasibility Cut From a Shortfall LP
The same first plan in 2031:

2031  need trans 15/14  distr  6/ 4  veget 11/ 2
      shortfall   6.50   sum of dual x bound   6.50
      nonzero duals: cover_distribution 1, own_distribution -1, over_distribution -1, cover_vegetation 1, own_vegetation -1, over_vegetation -1, pool -1
      feasibility cut: 1 need_distr(x) + 1 need_veget(x) -10.5 <= 0

Vegetation needs 11 crew-months against 2 of its own, 0.5 of overtime and a pool of 3 shared with distribution, which is itself 1 month short. No staffing covers it: $`Q_{2031}(\hat x) = +\infty`$, and no optimality cut can say so. The master needs a row that forbids this plan, and every plan that fails for the same reason: a **feasibility cut**.

The textbook route reads a **dual ray** of the infeasible LP (a Farkas certificate: prices that prove no solution exists). MathOpt's GLOP and HiGHS do not return one here, on a deliberately infeasible one-year LP:

GLOP  INFEASIBLE dual ray: False
HIGHS INFEASIBLE dual ray: False
PDLP  INFEASIBLE dual ray: True  cover 10601.4, own -10765.2, pool -10762.0

PDLP, a first-order method, returns one, but its numbers are those of an approximate method, and lesson 9.1.1 met the same gap for primal rays. The course uses a route that needs no ray and works with any LP solver: the **shortfall LP**. Add a variable $`s_g \ge 0`$ to each cover row, $`w_g + o_g + h_g + s_g \ge \text{need}_g`$, and minimize $`\sum_g s_g`$ instead of cost. It is always feasible (put all the need in $`s`$), and its optimum is zero exactly when the year can be covered. When it is positive, its duals $`\sigma`$ make the same argument as before: for every plan, the least shortfall is at least $`\sum_r \sigma_r\, \text{bound}_r(x)`$, so a plan with that sum above zero cannot be covered. The feasibility cut is
\sum_{g} \Bigl(\sigma_{\text{cover}_g}\, \text{need}_{g,y}(x) + \sigma_{\text{own}_g}\, K_{g,y} + \sigma_{\text{over}_g}\, \rho K_{g,y}\Bigr) + \sigma_{\text{pool}}\, U \;\le\; 0

Here it reads $`\text{need}_{\text{dist},2031}(x) + \text{need}_{\text{veg},2031}(x) \le 10.5`$: distribution and vegetation together cannot need more than their own crews (4 + 2), their overtime (1 + 0.5) and the pool (3). A planner would have written that rule by hand, had they known it was the one that binds. Benders found it from one infeasible plan.

m, rows = year_lp(portfolio, y, {g: need[g, y] for g in PROGRAMS}, phase_one=True)
short = mathopt.solve(m, mathopt.SolverType.GLOP)
if short.objective_value() > TOL:                  # no crews can cover this year's work
    cap.model.add_linear_constraint(cut_expression(short, rows, need_x, crews) <= 0,
                                    name=f"feas_{y}_{k}")
The Master Is an Upper Bound, Each Plan's True Value a Lower Bound; Stop When They Meet

The **master** is the plan model with a variable $`\theta_y \ge 0`$ per year and the objective $`\max \sum \text{npv}\,x - \sum_y \theta_y`$, plus every cut found so far. It starts with no cuts, so it believes crews are free.

items: The master's optimum is an **upper bound** on the whole model: every cut is valid for every plan, so the master is a relaxation, and adding cuts can only lower it.
Each plan the master proposes has a **true value**, $`\sum \text{npv}\,\hat x - \sum_y Q_y(\hat x)`$, when every year can be covered. That is a feasible plan's value, a **lower bound**.
When the master's $`\theta_y`$ already equal the $`Q_y(\hat x)`$, no cut is added: the master's value is the true value of a feasible plan, the two bounds meet, and the plan is optimal.

blocks.text: The loop re-solves the master from scratch each time (lesson 4.3.4's incremental edit, then a new solve); the next section says why not inside one search.

for k in range(1, max_iterations + 1):
    master = solve_highs(cap.model, EXACT)
    upper = master.objective_value()
    plan = schedule(cap, master)
    need = need_of(portfolio, plan)

m, rows = year_lp(portfolio, y, {g: need[g, y] for g in PROGRAMS})
sub = mathopt.solve(m, mathopt.SolverType.GLOP)
if total is not None:
    total += sub.objective_value()
if master.variable_values(theta[y]) < sub.objective_value() - TOL:
    cap.model.add_linear_constraint(theta[y] >= cut_expression(sub, rows, need_x, crews),
                                    name=f"opt_{y}_{k}")

iter  1  master (upper)  24,260.00  best plan (lower)       none  cuts: feasibility 1, optimality 2
iter  2  master (upper)  24,062.00  best plan (lower)       none  cuts: feasibility 2, optimality 1
iter  3  master (upper)  23,994.75  best plan (lower)  23,812.25  cuts: feasibility 0, optimality 1
iter  4  master (upper)  23,945.50  best plan (lower)  23,812.25  cuts: feasibility 1, optimality 3
iter  5  master (upper)  23,818.50  best plan (lower)  23,812.25  cuts: feasibility 0, optimality 1
iter  6  master (upper)  23,812.25  best plan (lower)  23,812.25  cuts: feasibility 0, optimality 0
Benders: 23,812.25 after 6 master solves;  monolithic MILP: 23,812.25
same plan: True   NPV 24,066  crew cost 253.75

The upper bound falls in every iteration, 24,260 to 23,812.25, as cuts accumulate. The first two plans cannot be staffed in some year, so there is no lower bound yet; the third plan can be, and its true value, 23,812.25, turns out to be the optimum, which the master proves three iterations later. Six master solves and 12 cuts in all reach the same value and the same plan as the monolithic MILP. The optimal plan gives up $194k of NPV (24,260 to 24,066) to cut the crew bill to $253.75k.

Two habits from this output carry over to any decomposition. **Compare against the monolithic solve** on an instance small enough to solve whole, and compare with a tolerance: HiGHS returns objective values with noise near $`10^{-5}`$, so a test of equality must allow for it (this module's tests use $`10^{-3}`$). And **report the bounds per iteration**, not only the final plan: a loop stopped early still gives an honest gap between its two bounds.
<!-- practice 2 -->
HiGHS Cannot Take the Cuts Inside Its Search; SCIP Can, as Lazy Constraints

Each master solve above starts the branch-and-bound search from scratch, and throws away a tree that already proved most of the answer. The alternative, often called **branch-and-Benders-cut**, solves the master once and adds each cut the moment an integer plan breaks it, as a **lazy constraint** (lesson 4.3.5). Lesson 4.3.5 showed that HiGHS through MathOpt accepts a lazy-constraint callback, never calls it, and returns plans that break the lazy rows. So the one-search version runs on SCIP, with the same cut function:

registration = mathopt.CallbackRegistration(events={mathopt.Event.MIP_SOLUTION}, add_lazy_constraints=True)
params = mathopt.SolveParameters(relative_gap_tolerance=0.0, threads=1, random_seed=1)
lazy = mathopt.solve(cap.model, mathopt.SolverType.GSCIP, params=params, callback_reg=registration, cb=separate)

one SCIP search with lazy cuts: OPTIMAL 23,812.25
monolithic MILP:                23,812.25
agree within 1e-3: True
cuts sent: {'feasibility': 6, 'optimality': 31}

One search reaches the same optimum. It sent 37 cuts, against the loop's 12, because SCIP calls the callback at every integer plan it meets, including plans the loop's master never proposed. Which version is faster depends on how costly a master solve is against a callback; the one search never throws a tree away, the loop never sends a cut for a plan that could not win. When this program runs, SCIP also writes two `[scip_event.c:305] ERROR` lines to the error stream; lesson 4.3.5 met them too, and the solve is unaffected.

So when the same callback is registered with HiGHS and the solve reports OPTIMAL above the loop's value, neither the cuts nor the loop is at fault. The cuts are not weaker in one search: sent by the same function to SCIP, they reach 23,812.25 above. The loop did not stop early: its two bounds met at 23,812.25, the monolithic MILP's value. HiGHS never called the callback, so it solved the master with no cuts, the master that believes crews are free, as in iteration 1 of the loop.
The Model
The Benders master after $`k`$ iterations, whole. New are the $`\theta_y`$ and the two kinds of cut; the crew variables and rows live only in the yearly subproblems.

**Sets, parameters.** As in the whole model above, plus $`\mathcal{O}_y`$, the optimality cuts found so far for year $`y`$, each with duals $`\pi^{(j)}`$, and $`\mathcal{F}_y`$, the feasibility cuts, each with shortfall duals $`\sigma^{(j)}`$.
**Variables.** $`x_{i,t} \in \{0,1\}`$ as before; $`\theta_y \ge 0`$ for every $`y \in Y`$, the master's estimate of year $`y`$'s crew cost ($k), continuous.
**Objective.**
\max \; \sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i} \text{npv}_{i,t}\, x_{i,t} \;-\; \sum_{y \in Y} \theta_y

**Constraints.** The once, must, alt, after and budget rows of lesson 11.3.1, and, writing $`\beta_y(\pi, x) = \sum_{g} (\pi_{\text{cover}_g} \text{need}_{g,y}(x) + \pi_{\text{own}_g} K_{g,y} + \pi_{\text{over}_g} \rho K_{g,y}) + \pi_{\text{pool}} U`$:

The **subproblem** of year $`y`$ at plan $`\hat x`$ is the LP $`Q_y(\hat x) = \min \sum_g (q^o o_g + q^c_g h_g)`$ over $`w, o, h \ge 0`$ subject to cover, own, over and pool with $`\text{need}_{g,y}(\hat x)`$ on the right; its **shortfall** version adds $`s_g \ge 0`$ to each cover row and minimizes $`\sum_g s_g`$.
Summary

items: **Fixing the integer plan leaves one small LP per year.** The continuous variables become a function $`Q_y(x)`$ of the plan, evaluated by an LP.

**The year's duals price its right-hand sides, and the same prices bound every other plan.** $`\theta_y \ge \sum_r \pi_r\, \text{bound}_r(x)`$ is exact at the plan that produced it and valid for every plan.
**An infeasible year returns a feasibility cut from a shortfall LP.** GLOP and HiGHS return no dual ray here; the shortfall LP's duals give the cut with any LP solver.
**The master is an upper bound, each plan's true value a lower bound; stop when they meet.** On GridCap small: 6 master solves, 12 cuts, the monolithic optimum 23,812.25 and the same plan.
**HiGHS cannot take the cuts inside its search; SCIP can, as lazy constraints.** One SCIP search sent 37 cuts and reached the same optimum.

blocks.text: Reference

rows: the integer part, with $`\theta_y`$ standing in for each subproblem's cost, plus the cuts so far
the LP left when the plan is fixed
$`\sum_r \sigma_r\, \text{bound}_r(x) \le 0`$ from a shortfall LP's duals (or a dual ray)
the master's optimum; falls as cuts are added
the best true value $`\sum \text{npv}\,\hat x - \sum_y Q_y(\hat x)`$ of a proposed plan
one master search, cuts added as lazy constraints at each integer plan
subproblems and shortfall LPs, with duals; no dual ray on an infeasible LP
the master in a loop of re-solves; never calls a callback (lesson 4.3.5)
the master as one search with lazy cuts (prints two `scip_event.c` lines)

blocks.text: **Further reading:** [OR-Tools MathOpt sample `tsp.py`](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/math_opt/samples/python/tsp.py) (the lazy-constraint pattern `benders_lazy.py` follows: a `MIP_SOLUTION` registration with `add_lazy_constraints=True`, and `add_lazy_constraint` for each row the candidate breaks; the sample itself runs on Gurobi); [MathOpt (OR-Tools)](https://developers.google.com/optimization/math_opt) (solving with GLOP, HiGHS and SCIP from one model); [Ralphs, *Integer Programming*, Lecture 20 (Lehigh ISE 418)](https://coral.ise.lehigh.edu/%7Eted/files/ie418/lectures/Lecture20.pdf) (Benders as projection onto the master variables through the subproblem's value function; optimality cuts from the subproblem's dual solutions, feasibility cuts from a dual ray, and the master's value as the upper bound that meets the subproblems' lower bound); [Hooker, *Logic-based Benders decomposition for large-scale optimization* (arXiv 1910.11944)](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1910.11944) (section 3, classical Benders as the case where the subproblem's inference dual is the LP dual; section 4, branch and check, which adds the cuts inside one master search); [Hybrid Lagrangian relaxation and Benders decomposition for stochastic hub location (University of Edinburgh)](https://www.research.ed.ac.uk/en/publications/a-hybrid-lagrangian-relaxation-and-benders-decomposition-algorith/) (a 2024 conference abstract: Benders on a two-stage stochastic model, combined with Lagrangian relaxation).
Challenges

items: Replace the five $`\theta_y`$ with one $`\theta`$ for the whole plan, and add one cut per iteration, the sum of the yearly ones. Predict whether the loop needs more or fewer master solves.
Raise the contractor pool from 3 to 30 crew-months. Predict which kind of cut disappears.

The first plan's 2031 feasibility cut is $`\text{need}_{\text{dist}} + \text{need}_{\text{veg}} \le 10.5`$. Why is transmission missing from it, although transmission also needs more than its own crews in 2031?
Write the cut that 2029's LP gives in words a crew manager would accept.

blocks.text: Design Note: Name Every Cut

Every cut the loop adds has a name, `opt_2029_1` or `feas_2031_1`: the year it bounds and the iteration that found it. When a master turns infeasible, or a plan is refused for a reason a planner cannot see, the names lead back to the plan and the year that produced the rule. Unnamed cuts make a decomposition a black box at exactly the moment someone needs to look inside.
The Full Programs

Each snippet above is part of a complete program, and each program printed the output the lesson shows. Open one to read it whole, change it, and run it again: Run starts the program on your copy of the code, so the course's own files never change.

**crew_costs.py.** The invented crew layer (overtime share, prices, contractor pool), each plan's crew need, and the yearly LP with its shortfall version (*Fixing the Integer Plan Leaves One Small LP per Year*). It prints nothing.

**first_cuts.py.** The first iteration by hand: each year's LP for the first master plan, the dual check, and the cut (*the second and third sections*). *Try:* Raise the vegetation contractor price from 25 to 35. Predict the new 2027 cut.
**dual_ray.py.** Asks GLOP, HiGHS and PDLP for a dual ray of an infeasible one-year LP (*An Infeasible Year Returns a Feasibility Cut*). *Try:* Raise the pool from 3 to 6. Predict every line.

**benders.py.** The Benders loop, the monolithic MILP, and the check that both give the same plan (*The Master Is an Upper Bound*). *Try:* Set `POOL` in `crew_costs.py` to 2. Predict whether the loop needs more master solves.

**benders_lazy.py.** The same cuts as lazy constraints in one SCIP search (*HiGHS Cannot Take the Cuts Inside Its Search*). *Try:* Register the callback with HiGHS instead of SCIP. Predict the objective, using lesson 4.3.5.
